_comment_family: The other end of the same family, and the pack kallisto-medium is the
other half of: read the note there first, because the reason both
declare a cut name instead of 'Kallisto' is stated once, in that one.
The short of it is that the file has done the splitting itself. Its
Windows records carry 'Kallisto Heavy' as name ID 1 and as the full
name ID 4, with the bare 'Kallisto' left in the typographic family
(ID 16), so the name declared here answers with this cut and the
Medium beside it cannot answer to it. That is what lets one channel
be set in both at once (see `highlight.face` in js/channels.js):
fontguard keys its check by family, so each cut is verified in its
own right and a missing one is named in the banner by itself.

_comment_css: Not declared in styles.css: this face arrived with a channel and is
registered from this JSON, which is the route content/README.md
describes. Nothing has to be added to the stylesheet for it.
_comment_local: What the machine may already know the face by, tried after the file.
The first is the Windows full name (name ID 4) and the second the
PostScript name (ID 6); both name this one cut rather than a family
with cuts in it, and the first is what the installer registers the
copy it puts in the user's font folder under (see
engine.install_fonts). 'Kallisto' on its own is deliberately absent:
it is the name the Medium answers to as well.
_comment_stack: The fallbacks are damage limitation and never a design choice - see
the longer note in kallisto-medium, which the reasoning here is the
heavy end of.
It lands somewhere better than that one does, and the numbers are why
this face gets its own list rather than the Medium's. Kallisto Heavy's
capitals average 0.768em; Arial Black's average 0.769em and Verdana
Bold's 0.765em. Both are within half a percent of the face they stand
in for, and both are black or bold cuts standing in for a 900 - which
is the rare case where a fallback keeps the weight AND the width, and
the picked words in a caption go on reading as picked words rather
than as a lighter face at a different size.
Arial Black leads because it is the 900 of the two and is on every
Windows this app runs on. Verdana Bold behind it for the width, then
Segoe UI - which at the declared 900 resolves to Segoe UI Black,
0.689em and the narrowest of the three, so it is last of the named
faces rather than first.
Impact is absent, alone among the heavy display faces a pack this
weight might reach for. At 0.509em it is a third narrower than what
these words were measured against: a picked word that came back in it
would not be a heavier word, it would be a shorter one.
